notes.meaning: "Ariel" is a name for Jerusalem, the city where King David lived. The name may mean "lion of God" or "altar hearth of God," the place where the altar fire always burned. God tells the city to go on keeping its yearly feasts and sacrifices. But a busy round of worship will not save people whose hearts and lives have not changed.

God himself will bring trouble on the city, and its feasting will turn to groaning and crying. Older writers read "like an altar hearth" in two ways. Some say the whole city will be like an altar covered with the blood of the slain. Others say the city will be like God's altar fire, which burns up the enemies who attack it. Matthew Henry notes that God says "distress," not "destroy": the trouble was meant to wake the people up and turn them back to him.

An enemy army will surround Jerusalem with towers and siege mounds. Yet God says, "I will camp around you." The Assyrians were only a tool in his hand. When people fight against us, we should ask what God is teaching us through it.

The proud city that once talked big will be brought down to the dust. It will only manage a weak whisper. That whisper is compared to the faint, eerie voice of mediums, who pretended to speak for the dead from under the ground. It was a fitting shame for a people who had gone to such mediums for advice.

Then comes a surprise. Jerusalem lay in the dust, but now its many enemies become like fine dust and blowing chaff, gone in a moment. The Lord comes with thunder, earthquake, storm and fire. Many link this to the night God's angel struck down the Assyrian army (Isaiah 37:36), and the storm words paint a picture of how sudden and fearful that judgment was. Some older writers, such as Calvin and Wesley, read these verses as still speaking against Jerusalem and the hired soldiers it trusted.

All the armies that attack Mount Zion will fade like a dream in the night. They are like a hungry man who dreams he is eating and wakes up still hungry. They were sure Jerusalem was theirs to take, but their hopes came to nothing. Matthew Henry sees this as a pattern: those who fight against God's people will be disappointed in the end.

Isaiah is amazed at how dull the people are. They act like drunks, but not from wine. They are spiritually numb and cannot see the danger they are in. They chose to close their eyes, and now that blindness becomes their punishment.

God has given them over to a deep sleep. This is his fair judgment on people who loved darkness more than light. Even the prophets and seers, who should have guided others, are blind. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 11:8.

God's message has become like a sealed scroll. The educated person says, "I can't read it, it's sealed." The uneducated person says, "I can't read." Both have an excuse, and neither is helped. Unless God opens the heart, no one truly understands. Matthew Henry says the Bible stays closed to anyone, learned or not, until they read it with a simple, teachable heart.

The people say the right words about God, but their hearts are far from him. Their worship follows rules made up by people instead of God's own word. Jesus quotes this verse against the religious leaders of his day (Matthew 15:8-9). Matthew Henry adds a comfort: a believer whose mind wanders in prayer is not the same as someone whose heart has turned away from God.

So God will do something astonishing: he will take wisdom away from the wise. They pulled their hearts away from God, so God pulls wisdom away from them. Their leaders will have no answers when trouble comes. Paul quotes this verse in 1 Corinthians 1:19.

Woe to those who make plans in secret and say, "Who sees us?" Many think this points to the leaders' secret plan to ask Egypt for help instead of trusting God, as Isaiah had urged. Underneath it lies a practical unbelief, as if God could not see everything.

They have turned things upside down, as if the clay could be the potter. Trying to hide from God is like a pot saying, "He didn't make me," or "He doesn't understand." The God who made us surely knows us. Their clever schemes are like clay in his hands.

Soon God will bring a great reversal. The wild forest of Lebanon will become a fruitful orchard, and today's orchard will look like a forest by comparison. Matthew Henry sees this first in the good years after the Assyrian army was defeated. Many also see it pointing to the gospel going to the Gentiles (non-Jews) while many in Israel turned away. Calvin reads it as a picture of the rich blessing God will pour out.

The sealed scroll of verse 11 is opened. People who were deaf to God's word will hear it, and people who were blind will see. This mainly means spiritual blindness healed by God's grace. Jesus did this for bodies and souls (Matthew 11:5).

The humble and the poor will find growing joy in the Lord, "the Holy One of Israel." Those who can rejoice in God even in hard times will soon have more reason to rejoice. Their joy comes as God shows himself to be their protector.

God will remove the bullies, the mockers and those who look for chances to do wrong. These people twisted a person's words to accuse him. They trapped anyone who spoke up at the city gate, where courts were held, and used false charges to crush innocent people. Isaiah likely had his own accusers in mind. Many also see the same pattern in those who tried to trap Jesus with words.

The God who rescued Abraham from the idol worship of Ur now speaks to Jacob's family. Jacob is pictured as an ancestor who has blushed and gone pale over his descendants' sins. That shame will end. The God who started his people with Abraham will not abandon them now.

Jacob will see his children, made new by God's own hand. They will "sanctify" God's name, meaning they will treat him as holy, and they will stand in awe of him. This is a new generation that truly honors God. Wesley sees Gentile believers joined with Israel among these children.

People who wandered in their thinking will come to understand, and grumblers will accept teaching. God does this by his Spirit, teaching the heart from the inside. Matthew Henry says this should encourage us to keep praying for those who have strayed.
